title: ClinVerse: A Realistic Multi-Agent Diagnostic Environment for Training and Evaluating Medical Agents
authors: Sirry Chen, Fangke Chen, Xuanwen Ding, Wei Chen, Zhongyu Wei
abstract: Disease diagnosis is a key application of large language model (LLM) agents in healthcare. However, existing medical agents are primarily trained and evaluated with static question-answering data, providing limited opportunities to learn active information acquisition, examination decision-making, and dynamic clinical interaction. To address this limitation, we present ClinVerse, an interactive, real-data-grounded multi-agent environment designed for training and evaluating medical diagnostic agents. Built on ClinPatient, a scalable dataset comprising 150k diagnostic cases derived from real-world electronic health records, ClinVerse supports coordinated interactions among six specialized clinical roles. Specifically, a doctor agent starts from an initial patient complaint, progressively gathers clinical evidence through patient interviews and examination requests, and ultimately produces a diagnosis. For each interaction trajectory, a rule-based scoring framework quantifies information acquisition, examination ordering, and diagnostic accuracy. These trajectory-level scores serve as reward signals for agent training while also enabling scalable evaluation. In experiments, we evaluate various general-purpose and medical-domain models and show that nine self-evolution methods across three categories consistently improve agents' diagnostic capabilities within ClinVerse. We further analyze the interplay among model capability, environment feedback, and self-evolution methods.

infographic.key_insight: ClinVerse moves medical-agent training and evaluation beyond static questions into interactive diagnostic simulations grounded in real-world health records.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The environment tests how AI agents gather patient information, request examinations, and form diagnoses, without establishing readiness for clinical use.
method: Supports coordinated interactions among six specialized clinical roles.
Doctor agents interview simulated patients and request examinations before diagnosing.
Rule-based trajectory scores measure information acquisition, examination ordering, and diagnostic accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Built on ClinPatient’s 150,000 EHR-derived diagnostic cases, ClinVerse evaluated general-purpose and medical models and reported improvements from nine self-evolution methods across three categories.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish whether gains in simulation translate to safe, effective performance in real clinical settings.
infographic.paper_title: ClinVerse: A Realistic Multi-Agent Diagnostic Environment for Training and Evaluating Medical Agents

title: DocTalk: Enhancing Medical Knowledge Retrieval via Fine-tuned Large Language Models with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Robust Clinical Decision Support
authors: Asad Gohar, Md Ariful Islam Mozumder, Moon-Il Joo, Hee-Cheol Kim
abstract: Objective: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare has opened new possibilities for AI-assisted clinical decision-making; however, safe and effective deployment remains challenging because of hallucination and domain misalignment. This study introduces DocTalk, a doctor-assistive question-answering (QA) system designed to generate concise, chart-grounded responses from de-identified discharge summaries. Methods: We developed a high-fidelity data generation pipeline that produces 500 clinically relevant QA pairs through sentence-level decomposition, chain-of-thought-guided question formulation, and expert review. Six open-source LLMs, including three general-purpose and three biomedical models, were evaluated before and after parameter-efficient instruction tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). The framework integrates prompt engineering, in-context learning, and medically aligned evaluation to support factual and interpretable responses. Results: On DocTalk-QA, instruction tuning produced consistent improvements across lexical, semantic, and clinical fidelity metrics. The best-performing tuned model, Llama-3-Med42-8B, achieved ROUGE-L = 0.40, BERTScore-F1 = 0.76, and UMLS-F1 = 0.49. To examine external generalization beyond the DocTalk-QA dataset, the two best-performing models, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3-Med42-8B, were evaluated on PubMedQA before and after instruction tuning. Accuracy improved from 0.931 to 0.977 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from 0.935 to 0.943 for Llama-3-Med42-8B. Conclusion: DocTalk was deployed as a secure web-based platform for interactive EHR querying. These findings suggest that clinically grounded instruction tuning can improve medical QA performance and support practical clinical decision support.

infographic.key_insight: DocTalk improved chart-grounded medical question answering through clinically aligned LoRA instruction tuning of open-source language models.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The system could help clinicians retrieve information from discharge summaries, though improved QA scores do not establish clinical safety or patient benefit.
method: Generated 500 QA pairs from de-identified discharge summaries using sentence-level decomposition, chain-of-thought-guided question formulation, and expert review.
Evaluated six general-purpose and biomedical LLMs before and after LoRA instruction tuning.
Tested the two leading models on PubMedQA and deployed an interactive EHR-querying web platform.
infographic.evidence_signal: The best tuned model achieved ROUGE-L 0.40, BERTScore-F1 0.76, and UMLS-F1 0.49; PubMedQA accuracy rose from 93.1% to 97.7% and from 93.5% to 94.3% for the two leading models.
infographic.watch_item: The 500-pair dataset and benchmark gains do not establish reliability in real-world clinical workflows; prospective safety validation remains necessary.
infographic.paper_title: DocTalk: Enhancing Medical Knowledge Retrieval via Fine-tuned Large Language Models with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Robust Clinical Decision Support

title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
authors: Wei-Wei Zhang, Pengkai Wang, Yan Li, Zhijie Sang, Guan-Qun Zhou, Jun-Yan Li
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promise in specialty medicine, yet existing evaluations largely focus on isolated clinical encounters rather than tracking how clinical responsibilities evolve across a longitudinal care pathway. Here we introduce NPC-RubricBench, a phase-aware benchmark for evaluating multistage clinical reasoning across the cancer care continuum, using nasopharyngeal carcinoma as a defined disease context. Curated from longitudinal records of 405 patients across two cancer centers, the benchmark comprises 941 patient-phase units across six sequential care phases and 17,688 patient-specific atomic criteria spanning five evaluation dimensions, with each assessment strictly restricted to decision-time clinical evidence. Evaluating 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs revealed that strong diagnostic performance does not carry over to downstream care. We evaluated 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs, showing that high diagnostic performance did not translate into improved downstream care. Instead, the dominant failure modes reversed across phases. Explicit decision errors dominated anatomical staging at 48.2%, whereas decision omissions dominated initial work-up and post-treatment follow-up at 33.4% and 30.4%, respectively. In the evaluated model set, medically adapted models showed higher omission rates than general-purpose models. Moreover, varying query granularity exposes a critical specification trade-off: broad open-ended requests degrade Decision Quality across all 30 models, while more detailed, checklist-like prompts raise Decision Quality but reduce Evidence Faithfulness and Safety Adherence. Furthermore, NPC-RubricBench demonstrates that static diagnostic benchmarks are insufficient to ensure consistent clinical reliability over time, highlighting the importance of phase-adaptive safeguards in multistage medical AI.

infographic.key_insight: Strong diagnostic performance did not ensure reliable downstream cancer-care reasoning, and dominant failure modes changed across care phases.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Evaluating medical AI across longitudinal care may reveal errors and omissions that isolated diagnostic benchmarks miss.
method: Built NPC-RubricBench from longitudinal nasopharyngeal carcinoma records across six care phases.
Scored 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs using patient-specific criteria restricted to decision-time evidence.
Varied prompt granularity to assess trade-offs in decision quality, evidence faithfulness, and safety adherence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark included 405 patients from two cancer centers, 941 patient-phase units, and 17,688 atomic criteria; explicit decision errors dominated staging at 48.2%, while omissions dominated initial work-up at 33.4% and follow-up at 30.4%.
infographic.watch_item: Results from one cancer type and two centers may not generalize to other settings, and benchmark performance does not establish clinical safety.
infographic.paper_title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care

title: PathKGen: Pathology Knowledge Assisted MLLM for Explainable Histopathology
authors: Nadun Rajapaksha, Sandun Herath, Devnith Wijesinghe, Isiri Amani Withanawasam, Hasindri Watawana, Ranga Rodrigo
abstract: Whole Slide Image (WSI) analysis serves as the fundamental method for the clinical diagnosis of cancer in digital histopathology. Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have enabled state-of-the-art (SOTA) automated histopathology report generation. However, MLLMs reason purely through distributions encoded in their neural parameters, limiting the amount of knowledge and reasoning logic they can contain given the model scale. Their black-box reasoning poses another challenge to the human interpretation of intermediate reasoning. We address these issues by utilizing knowledge graphs to inject external structured knowledge for MLLMs to reason over, while making this reasoning component visible. Knowledge graphs are capable of partially externalizing the containment of medical knowledge, an area that remains underexplored in pathology report generation. We introduce PathKGen, a knowledge graph-assisted MLLM for histopathology report generation. PathKGen has two main branches: (1) a visual path that learns visual token inputs to the MLLM using pathology foundation models, and (2) a knowledge path that learns knowledge token inputs by extracting key morphological features of WSIs through querying a pathology-specific knowledge graph. A comprehensive evaluation on WSI-Bench dataset shows that PathKGen surpasses previous SOTA methods while revealing diagnostic reasoning as visually intuitive graphs. Due to its modular design, the proposed knowledge path is complementary to vision-aligned MLLMs and can be extended to other applications by curating domain-specific knowledge graphs to generate knowledge tokens.

infographic.key_insight: PathKGen combines visual features with structured pathology knowledge to generate histopathology reports and expose its knowledge-based reasoning as graphs.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support more interpretable automated pathology reporting, but the abstract does not establish clinical readiness.
method: A visual branch uses pathology foundation models to produce visual tokens.
A knowledge branch queries a pathology-specific knowledge graph for key morphological features and produces knowledge tokens.
A multimodal large language model uses both token streams to generate reports.
infographic.evidence_signal: On WSI-Bench, the authors report outperforming previous state-of-the-art methods, though the abstract provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Visible reasoning graphs do not guarantee correct reports; performance may depend on the knowledge graph’s accuracy and coverage.
infographic.paper_title: PathKGen: Pathology Knowledge Assisted MLLM for Explainable Histopathology

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
abstract: Recently, there has been rise in multimodal vision-language models for computer-aided diagnosis (CAD), yet their application in breast diagnosis, particularly for predicting biopsy outcomes remains limited. This study presents a multimodal vision-language approach, incorporating Grad-CAM as an Explainable AI (XAI) technique, to predict benign tumors in patients recommended for biopsy, especially those classified as BI-RADS 4 and 5. A novel multimodal framework was devel- oped using Vision Transformer (ViT) for imaging feature extraction and DeBERTa-V3-Large for textual embeddings. The model was trained and evaluated on a comprehensive in-house dataset comprising 1,632 patients, each with four mammography views and a corresponding radiology report. The features of both modalities were extracted independently and fused by late fusion before classification. Grad-CAM was used to generate visual explanations highlighting key regions influencing model predictions. The proposed model demonstrated high sensitivity 90%, 95%, 99%, and 100% with corresponding specificities of 40%, 36%, 18%, and 11%, respectively. The best AUC achieved was 0.72 by multimodal approach on the test set, outperforming the image only (0.66) and text-only (0.68) baselines. The proposed multimodal architecture, enhanced with Grad-CAM, demonstrates a strong potential to identify benign tumors among high-risk patients, offering interpretable insights and thereby helping reduce unnecessary biopsies, patient anxiety, and healthcare costs.

infographic.key_insight: Combining mammograms and radiology reports improved biopsy-outcome discrimination over either modality alone, with a test AUC of 0.72.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could help identify benign findings among patients recommended for biopsy, particularly BI-RADS 4–5, but clinical benefit remains unproven.
method: Vision Transformer extracted features from four mammography views per patient.
DeBERTa-V3-Large encoded radiology reports; late fusion combined image and text features.
Grad-CAM highlighted image regions influencing predictions.
infographic.evidence_signal: An in-house dataset included 1,632 patients; test AUCs were 0.72 for multimodal, 0.66 for image-only, and 0.68 for text-only models, with 18% specificity at 99% sensitivity.
infographic.watch_item: External validation and prospective safety evaluation are needed before using predictions to defer biopsies.
infographic.paper_title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
abstract: Clinical expertise is inherently distributed: it resides not in any single dataset or institution but in the accumulated reasoning experiences of thousands of clinicians navigating diverse patient populations, resource constraints, and evolving treatment protocols. Yet current approaches to scaling medical AI, from centralized large language models to federated learning, remain anchored to a data-centric paradigm that treats knowledge as static parameters to be aggregated. In this Perspective, we argue for a fundamental shift from data aggregation to experience aggregation. We propose Decentralized Agentic Systems (DAS), a framework in which distributed AI agents operating across healthcare institutions synthesize collective clinical intelligence by sharing abstracted reasoning trajectories rather than raw data or model parameters. Unlike federated learning, which averages numerical gradients across homogeneous model architectures, DAS exchanges structured records of clinical reasoning, specifically the sequence of observations, hypotheses, tool invocations, and outcome feedback that constitute diagnostic experience. We examine the architectural principles, deployment considerations, governance requirements, and critical open challenges of this framework, laying the groundwork for a collaborative medical AI ecosystem where distributed expertise autonomously adapts to the complexities of longitudinal patient care.

infographic.key_insight: This Perspective proposes Decentralized Agentic Systems (DAS) to build collective clinical intelligence by sharing abstracted reasoning experiences rather than raw data or model parameters.
infographic.clinical_relevance: DAS could help healthcare institutions learn from diverse clinical experiences and adapt AI support to longitudinal care.
method: Connect distributed AI agents across healthcare institutions.
Exchange structured reasoning trajectories: observations, hypotheses, tool use, and outcome feedback.
Aggregate experiences rather than numerical model updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a conceptual framework and discusses deployment and governance, but reports no datasets, empirical evaluation, or clinical outcomes.
infographic.watch_item: Sharing abstracted reasoning still requires privacy safeguards and validation before clinical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence

title: Acute Stroke Classification Using Asymmetric Data Standardization and Orthogonal-Focal Loss Optimized CNN-ViT Cross-Attention Fusion: A Multicenter External Validation Study
authors: Tansel Uyar
abstract: Background/Objectives: Rapid differentiation of ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke subtypes is vital for acute management. Although current deep learning models achieve high single-dataset accuracy, they suffer from "shortcut learning" and domain shift in external validation. This study proposes a hierarchical computer-aided diagnostic (CAD) system mimicking emergency triage. Methods: We introduce a 3-channel Radiology-Focused Preprocessing pipeline that feeds radiological Hounsfield Unit (HU) windows into Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Vision Transformer (ViT) backbones via asymmetric formats (.mat and .png). The architecture utilizes a novel joint cross-attention fusion network optimized by an Integrated Orthogonal-Focal Loss. Results: Our system achieved a 95.48% F1-score on the internal stroke dataset. However, multi-center external validation (AISD, BHSD, PhysioNet) using a Mask Anchor filter revealed a drop to the 58-62% range, exposing the "internal validation illusion" caused by hardware noise. Critically, models exhibited high precision (77%) but low sensitivity (57%) for ischemic stroke, proving prone to hemorrhage overdiagnosis. Multi-seed variance analysis demonstrated that the DenseNet201+ViT backbone yielded the lowest deviation (0.59) and highest stability, making it the most reliable architecture for real-world clinical integration. Conclusions: To overcome diagnostic challenges, future research must focus on multimodal architectures that combine 3D volumetric extraction with clinical data.

infographic.key_insight: Strong internal stroke-classification performance did not generalize: F1 fell from 95.48% internally to approximately 58–62% in multicenter external validation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Low ischemic-stroke sensitivity and a tendency to overdiagnose hemorrhage raise concerns about reliability in acute stroke triage.
method: Three-channel CT preprocessing used radiological Hounsfield Unit windows and asymmetric .mat/.png formats.
CNN and Vision Transformer features were combined through cross-attention fusion with Integrated Orthogonal-Focal Loss.
External evaluation used a Mask Anchor filter, while multi-seed analysis assessed model stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: External testing on AISD, BHSD, and PhysioNet showed ischemic-stroke precision of 77% but sensitivity of 57%; DenseNet201+ViT had the lowest reported multi-seed deviation (0.59).
infographic.watch_item: Low variability across seeds does not establish clinical readiness, especially given the large external-performance drop and missed ischemic strokes.
infographic.paper_title: Acute Stroke Classification Using Asymmetric Data Standardization and Orthogonal-Focal Loss Optimized CNN-ViT Cross-Attention Fusion: A Multicenter External Validation Study

title: Evaluating Bayesian deep learning for robust biomedical time-series classification under distribution shift: A sleep scoring case study
authors: Mads Birch Sørensen, Ulrike Richter, Francois Gastambide, Michael Riis Andersen
abstract: In biomedical time-series classification, machine learning models often suffer from deteriorating accuracy and calibration due to distribution shift. We investigate to what degree Bayesian-inspired deep learning improves robustness through Bayesian model averaging (BMA). Using rodent sleep scoring as a case study, we evaluate BMA under distribution shifts in genotype, laboratory, and species. We systematically compare nine approximate inference methods spanning single- and multi-basin approaches across two neural network backbones on in-distribution (ID) data and five out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets. In our results, multi-basin methods perform best, outperforming baselines and single-basin methods. Compared with point estimates, BMA generally improves OOD accuracy and calibration across both architectures, while yielding only modest ID gains. It also often improves selective prediction and OOD and artifact detection, but, interestingly, not inter-rater disagreement detection.

infographic.key_insight: Bayesian model averaging generally improved sleep-scoring accuracy and calibration under distribution shift, with multi-basin methods performing best.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The findings suggest potential for more reliable biomedical time-series classification across changing data sources, but do not establish clinical benefit in humans.
method: Used rodent sleep scoring as a biomedical time-series case study.
Compared nine approximate inference methods across two neural network backbones.
Tested robustness to genotype, laboratory, and species shifts.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covered in-distribution data and five out-of-distribution datasets; gains were modest in-distribution and generally larger under shift.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits were not universal: Bayesian model averaging did not improve inter-rater disagreement detection.
infographic.paper_title: Evaluating Bayesian deep learning for robust biomedical time-series classification under distribution shift: A sleep scoring case study

title: Overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1: Patient-Specific Phenotype Concept Recognition in Full-Text Biomedical Literature
authors: Xuanlyu Zhu, Feng Tian, Yang Zhong, Pengqi Zheng, Xiwen Bi, Ling Luo
abstract: Automatic phenotype information extraction plays an important role in rare disease diagnosis, genotype-phenotype analysis, and precision medicine. However, accurately identifying phenotype concepts and determining their associations with specific patients remain challenging, particularly in full-text biomedical articles involving multiple patients and complex clinical descriptions. This paper presents an overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1, which aims to promote the development of methods for patient-specific phenotype concept recognition from full-text biomedical literature. The task consists of two subtasks: full-text phenotype concept recognition and patient-specific phenotype association. For this evaluation, we used 200 annotated full-text biomedical articles from the PatientPheX dataset, containing 506 patients, 15,193 phenotype mentions, and 5,656 patient-phenotype associations. A total of 455 teams registered for the competition, with 189 and 103 valid submissions received on the Phase A and Phase B leaderboards, respectively. The best-performing system achieved an overall score of 0.7389 on the final test set, outperforming the baseline by 8.37 percentage points. The top-performing teams explored diverse approaches combining biomedical language models, large language models (LLMs), and ensemble strategies. The evaluation results highlight both the potential of these approaches and the remaining challenges in patient attribution and phenotype normalization from full-text biomedical literature. The post-evaluation phase remains open at https://tianchi.aliyun.com/competition/entrance/532512.

infographic.key_insight: The best system linked phenotype concepts to individual patients in full-text biomedical articles with an overall score of 0.7389, exceeding the baseline by 8.37 percentage points.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Patient-specific phenotype extraction could support rare disease research and genotype–phenotype analysis, but clinical utility was not evaluated.
method: Recognize phenotype concepts in full-text biomedical literature.
Associate phenotype concepts with specific patients.
Top teams explored biomedical language models, LLMs, and ensemble strategies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark used 200 annotated PatientPheX articles covering 506 patients, 15,193 phenotype mentions, and 5,656 patient–phenotype associations.
infographic.watch_item: Patient attribution and phenotype normalization remain challenging, particularly in articles describing multiple patients.
infographic.paper_title: Overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1: Patient-Specific Phenotype Concept Recognition in Full-Text Biomedical Literature

title: Visualizing and Interpreting Temporal Care Team Dynamics for Cancer Survival Risk Analysis
authors: Yuhua Huang, Hsiao-Ying Lu, Kwan-Liu Ma
abstract: Cancer care is a longitudinal, time-sensitive process requiring coordination among diverse healthcare professionals (HCPs), whose collaboration evolves throughout treatment. Prior studies link care team structure to patient outcomes, but the temporal dynamics of collaboration and their relationship to evolving patient risk remain poorly understood. We introduce a visual analytics framework for modeling and interpreting time-varying care team interactions in oncology. We construct dynamic collaboration networks from electronic health record (EHR)-mediated communication data and use a temporal graph neural network (TGNN) to estimate patient outcome risk over time. We then investigate how changes in care team composition and specialist participation relate to shifts in estimated risk across treatment stages. Our multi-view interactive system combines TGNN-based risk modeling with coordinated visualizations of care team networks, feature-level explanations from a surrogate logistic regression model, and exploratory what-if analysis. Without making causal claims, the system helps analysts examine how risk estimates co-evolve with collaboration patterns and identify care team characteristics associated with these changes. We demonstrate its utility through expert-guided analysis scenarios involving 505 patients with breast, colorectal, and lung cancers, evaluating its ability to reveal clinically meaningful collaboration patterns. This work improves the interpretability of temporal graph-based models in longitudinal, team-based healthcare, with potential applicability to other evolving collaborative settings.

infographic.key_insight: An interactive visual analytics framework links evolving cancer care team collaboration patterns with model-estimated patient outcome risk, without implying causation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework may help analysts explore how care team composition and specialist participation relate to changing risk estimates across cancer treatment stages.
method: Build dynamic care team networks from EHR-mediated communications.
Estimate outcome risk over time using a temporal graph neural network.
Combine network visualizations, surrogate logistic regression explanations, and exploratory what-if analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Expert-guided analysis scenarios involved 505 patients with breast, colorectal, and lung cancers; the abstract reports no quantitative predictive performance.
infographic.watch_item: Observed associations and what-if outputs do not establish that changing care team composition would improve survival.
infographic.paper_title: Visualizing and Interpreting Temporal Care Team Dynamics for Cancer Survival Risk Analysis

title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Liver Lesion Segmentation and Structured Radiology Reporting
authors: Fatma Ahmed Mansour, Rahatara Ferdousi, Manar Fathy Elshenawy
abstract: Despite advances in automated liver lesion segmentation, a gap remains between image-derived predictions and clinically interpretable radiology reports. Bridging this gap requires quantitative measurements that are both reproducible and traceable. We present an evidence-grounded agentic AI framework that connects liver and lesion segmentation with deterministic quantification and structured reporting. TotalSegmentator-based nnU-Net models delineate the liver, Couinaud segments, and lesions, while computational tools extract volumes, dimensions, counts, and anatomical locations. A large language model (LLM) organizes these measurements into a predefined reporting schema, with numerical consistency checks against source measurements. On 51 LiTS cases, the segmentation stage achieved a liver Dice score of 0.947, lesion sensitivity of 75.6%, and positive predictive value of 68.9%. Exploratory screening of 25,494 MERLIN reports identified 10,208 (40.0%) with liver-related abnormalities. By connecting quantitative imaging evidence with agentic report generation, this work takes a step toward human-centered medical AI that prioritizes traceability and clinical relevance.

infographic.key_insight: An agentic AI workflow links liver lesion segmentation to structured radiology reports grounded in traceable, computed measurements.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could help translate imaging predictions into interpretable reports while preserving links to quantitative evidence.
method: TotalSegmentator-based nnU-Net models segment the liver, Couinaud segments, and lesions.
Computational tools calculate volumes, dimensions, lesion counts, and anatomical locations.
An LLM organizes measurements into a predefined report schema, with numerical consistency checks.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 51 LiTS cases, segmentation achieved liver Dice 0.947, lesion sensitivity 75.6%, and positive predictive value 68.9%; separate exploratory screening identified liver-related abnormalities in 10,208 of 25,494 MERLIN reports (40.0%).
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish clinical reporting accuracy or workflow benefit, and segmentation errors could propagate into reports.
infographic.paper_title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Liver Lesion Segmentation and Structured Radiology Reporting

title: AI-Empowered Multimodal Data Integration and Knowledge Discovery for Pharmacovigilance
authors: Li, Y.; Zhou, H.; Yeh, F.-Y.; Sun, Z.; Zheng, J.; Alzaidi, S.; Guan, H.; Li, J.; Seger, D. L.; Wang, L.; Li, M.; Li, X.; Chen, T.; Plasek, J. M.; Li, H.; Jiang, A.; Hong, P.; Li, F.; Zhang, W.; Cui, L.; Bates, D. W.; Zhou, L.; He, Y.; Tao, C.
abstract: Biomedical artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly relies on heterogeneous data sources, yet differences in data structure, terminology, evidence quality, and provenance complicate their integration into reliable knowledge resources. Here, we develop an evidence-aware framework for processing and integrating heterogeneous pharmacovigilance data from FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) reports, biomedical literature, clinical trials, and electronic health records in Mass General Brigham. The framework combines large language model (LLM)-based information extraction, ontology-driven semantic normalization, cross-source evidence assessment, statistical and machine learning-based prioritization, and ingredient-based adverse drug event (ADE) relationship inference to transform heterogeneous evidence into a structured and evidence-based knowledge resource. The constructed knowledge system contains 11,588 drug nodes, 44,843 ingredient nodes, 3,275 ADE nodes, 993 indication nodes, and more than 2.47 million relationships, with each drug-ADE relationship assigned a confidence score. We further developed a drug-level web interface for accessing the knowledge resource and validated its utility in downstream AI tasks. Specifically, incorporating the developed knowledge resource improved the comprehensiveness, relevance, and overall quality of LLM-based drug-specific ADE synthesis and improved the precision and F1 score of clinical ADE relation extraction. These results demonstrate that AI-assisted processing combined with evidence-aware curation can transform heterogeneous biomedical evidence into reusable, AI-ready knowledge with explicit provenance and evidence strength information. The framework provides a general strategy for integrating heterogeneous biomedical data to support reproducible knowledge construction and downstream biomedical AI applications.

infographic.key_insight: An evidence-aware AI framework integrates diverse pharmacovigilance sources into a knowledge resource that improved downstream adverse drug event (ADE) synthesis and extraction.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The resource could support drug-safety research by making ADE evidence, provenance, and confidence more accessible, but clinical benefit was not established.
method: Integrate FAERS reports, biomedical literature, clinical trials, and Mass General Brigham electronic health records.
Combine LLM extraction, ontology-based normalization, and cross-source evidence assessment.
Prioritize relationships using statistical and machine learning methods and infer ADE links through drug ingredients.
infographic.evidence_signal: The resource contains over 2.47 million relationships; evaluations reported better LLM ADE synthesis quality and higher clinical ADE extraction precision and F1, without numerical gains in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: Confidence-scored drug–ADE links should not be treated as causal findings; the abstract does not establish prospective clinical safety or effectiveness.
infographic.paper_title: AI-Empowered Multimodal Data Integration and Knowledge Discovery for Pharmacovigilance

title: A Visual Grounding Benchmark for Retinal OCT with Multimodal Large Language Models
authors: Ronald Fecso, José Morano, Botond Fazekas, Paul Widmann-Sedlnitzky, Dorota Himel, Laetita Hinterhuber
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can answer clinical questions about medical images, but trustworthy use requires visual grounding: models should localize the pathology they report rather than rely on spurious shortcuts. Whether MLLMs can visually ground clinical findings in retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT), the most widely used imaging modality in ophthalmology, remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce RetinaGroundBench, the first benchmark for biomarker visual grounding in retinal OCT. It comprises 815 B-scans exhaustively annotated by ophthalmologists with 4,537 bounding boxes covering 13 biomarkers across 8 diseases. Because MLLMs often fragment a single lesion into multiple partial predictions, we propose AggIoU, a metric that evaluates whether the union of overlapping predicted boxes covers the annotated region. Across 27 open-source MLLMs (0.8-38B parameters), we find that visual grounding remains largely unsolved: the best general-purpose model achieves a macro F1 of just 23.7%, with consistently low recall, despite reaching up to 73% balanced accuracy on biomarker presence questions. To narrow this gap, we developed RetGrounder, an MLLM fine-tuned using an OCT-specific strategy integrating grounding and textual information. Despite its relatively small size (8B), RetGrounder improves grounding F1 to 33.9%, a 43% relative improvement. Our benchmark provides a reference point for measuring progress in the field of OCT diagnosis with MLLMs.

infographic.key_insight: MLLMs struggle to localize retinal OCT biomarkers, but OCT-specific fine-tuning raised grounding F1 from 23.7% to 33.9%.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Localizing reported findings could make image-based AI outputs easier to verify, but these results do not establish readiness for clinical use.
method: Introduced RetinaGroundBench with ophthalmologist-annotated biomarker bounding boxes.
Proposed AggIoU to assess combined coverage from overlapping predicted boxes.
Evaluated 27 open-source MLLMs and fine-tuned the 8B-parameter RetGrounder using OCT grounding and text.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark includes 815 B-scans, 4,537 bounding boxes, 13 biomarkers and 8 diseases; RetGrounder achieved 33.9% grounding F1 versus 23.7% for the best general-purpose model, a 43% relative improvement.
infographic.watch_item: Grounding performance remains limited, and biomarker presence accuracy should not be mistaken for reliable localization.
infographic.paper_title: A Visual Grounding Benchmark for Retinal OCT with Multimodal Large Language Models

title: Can JEV Support Clinical Trial Criteria Assessment?
authors: Mengxian He, Ziyue Gao, Chun Li, Shunyi Zhang, Hao Wei, Minqing Zhang
abstract: Clinical trial prescreening requires distinguishing unmet conditions from insufficient evidence in patient records. Given patient records, criterion questions, and predefined answer options, we retrospectively compared JEV, a non-generative decision model returning native option probabilities, with schema-constrained Qwen Flash across 2,048 test patient-condition pairs from TrialGPT and question-answer datasets derived from MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, all evaluated under strict Zero Data Retention (ZDR) policies to ensure clinical data privacy. Both models assessed conditions individually or in batches sharing the same patient context, with performance measured against reference labels. In batch mode, JEV and Qwen achieved similar macro-F1 scores on TrialGPT (0.652 vs. 0.660) and MIMIC-IV (0.807 vs. 0.814), whereas JEV substantially outperformed Qwen on MIMIC-III (0.768 vs. 0.534; $Δ$ = +0.234, 95% CI: 0.187-0.281). This advantage largely reflected higher recall for conditions labeled as having insufficient information (56.3% vs. 9.9%). Across all three datasets, JEV also had lower observed median job latency (1.18-1.40 vs. 2.80-8.90 s) and 53%-74% lower estimated cost per condition. These findings position JEV as an initial assessment component that provides criterion-level judgments and flags potential information gaps for review. JEV's observed errors in interpreting clinical evidence underscore the need to verify its outputs against patient records before they inform eligibility decisions.

infographic.key_insight: JEV matched Qwen Flash’s batch-mode macro-F1 on two datasets and outperformed it on MIMIC-III, with lower observed latency and estimated cost.
infographic.clinical_relevance: JEV could support trial prescreening by assessing individual criteria and flagging information gaps for human review.
method: Retrospectively evaluated 2,048 patient-condition pairs from TrialGPT and MIMIC-III/IV-derived question-answer datasets.
Compared non-generative JEV with schema-constrained Qwen Flash in individual and shared-context batch modes.
Measured performance against reference labels under strict Zero Data Retention policies.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MIMIC-III in batch mode, JEV achieved macro-F1 of 0.768 versus 0.534 (difference: +0.234; 95% CI: 0.187–0.281), with higher recall for insufficient-information labels (56.3% versus 9.9%).
infographic.watch_item: This retrospective evaluation does not establish clinical readiness; evidence-interpretation errors require verification against patient records before eligibility decisions.
infographic.paper_title: Can JEV Support Clinical Trial Criteria Assessment?

title: Gender Associations in LLM-Mediated ADHD Self-Diagnosis
authors: Matilde Elene Hansen, Ross Deans Kristensen-McLachlan
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for medical self-diagnosis. However, the way demographic cues shape outputs in these interactions remains poorly understood. This is particularly consequential for diagnoses like ADHD, where persistent gender disparities are not fully aligned with the clinical evidence. We adapt the Context Association Test (CAT) to evaluate whether GPT-4o responds to gendered ADHD associations in a zero-shot, self-diagnostic setting. We show that explicit cueing consistently amplifies certain ADHD subtype associations while implicit cueing produces near proxy-aligned distributions. These divergences suggest that explicit demographic cues may activate bias-mitigation mechanisms that over-correct rather than eliminate bias, whereas implicit cues appear to reflect the model's default behavior. Our results demonstrate that evaluating gendered bias in LLM-mediated self-diagnosis requires careful attention to the demographic associations a model encodes.

infographic.key_insight: GPT-4o’s gendered ADHD subtype associations differed between explicit and implicit cues, suggesting that cue framing can shape bias in self-diagnostic interactions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Gender-sensitive responses could influence users’ understanding of ADHD, underscoring the need to evaluate demographic bias in medical AI tools.
method: Adapted the Context Association Test to ADHD self-diagnosis.
Evaluated GPT-4o in a zero-shot setting.
Compared ADHD associations under explicit and implicit gender cues.
infographic.evidence_signal: Explicit cues consistently amplified certain ADHD subtype associations, while implicit cues produced distributions close to the study’s proxy reference.
infographic.watch_item: Bias-mitigation overcorrection is a proposed explanation, not a demonstrated mechanism; the abstract does not establish diagnostic accuracy or patient outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: Gender Associations in LLM-Mediated ADHD Self-Diagnosis

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
abstract: Vision Transformer (ViT) classifiers commonly rely on a global classification (CLS) token for image-level prediction, which is poorly aligned with local interpretability requirements in medical imaging. We propose SAP-ViT, a Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer that replaces CLS-based classification with direct aggregation of last-layer patch embeddings. This design makes class predictions decomposable into patch-level contributions as part of the forward pass. To encourage concise and readable evidence, SAP-ViT applies sparsity regularization to the patch-weight distribution. Since self-attention mixes information across patch tokens, we further introduce an input-space back-mapping mechanism to estimate which input patches contribute to influential output patch embeddings. We evaluate SAP-ViT qualitatively and quantitatively on multiple medical image classification datasets spanning different imaging modalities. The results show that SAP-ViT maintains strong classification performance while providing consistent and interpretable patch-level explanations across datasets. Ablation results further show that both sparsity regularization and the alignment component of input-space back-mapping contribute to the final explanation quality. Overall, SAP-ViT provides a favorable trade-off between predictive accuracy and interpretability for ViT-based medical image classification.

infographic.key_insight: SAP-ViT replaces CLS-token classification with patch-embedding aggregation, making predictions decomposable into patch-level contributions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Patch-level explanations could help researchers inspect image evidence behind medical image classifications, but clinical utility is not established.
method: Aggregate final-layer patch embeddings directly for classification.
Apply sparsity regularization to encourage concise patch-level evidence.
Estimate input-patch contributions through back-mapping that accounts for attention mixing.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across multiple medical imaging datasets and modalities, the abstract reports strong classification performance and interpretable explanations, with ablations supporting sparsity regularization and back-mapping alignment.
infographic.watch_item: Back-mapping estimates input contributions; the abstract provides no numerical results or clinical validation.
infographic.paper_title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification

title: Auditing evaluation artifacts and data leakage in large language model systems for rare disease diagnosis
authors: Jian Yang, Peilin Liu, Xiaohan Li, Songda Li, Yu Cao, Yuqing Feng
abstract: Augmented large language model (LLM) systems have reported high benchmark accuracies in rare disease diagnosis, yet their real-world clinical utility remains unproven. A recent meta-analysis flagged augmented LLM diagnostic evaluations as having a high risk of bias due to suspected data leakage; however, the precise impact of these vulnerabilities on model inference has yet to be fully quantified. In this study, we present a comprehensive empirical audit to quantify evaluation artifacts across prevailing AI paradigms, using a repository of over 60,000 cases from diverse public and independent clinical cohorts. By reconstructing a state-of-the-art agentic framework, we demonstrate that candidate-space contamination artificially inflates performance: enforcing strict cross-dataset isolation resulted in a marked performance decline, with the cross-dataset mean Recall@1 decreasing from 54.3% (under conventional one-vs-rest evaluation) to 40.3% (Hedges' g = 0.94). Similar spatial overfitting in supervised classifiers caused diagnostic accuracy to drop from an internal mean of 42.9% to 16.7% across external cohorts (Cohen's d = 2.01). Furthermore, we quantify how LLMs infer diagnoses by exploiting retrospective therapeutic cues in clinical narratives, and how temporal misalignment in foundational knowledge bases leads to performance fluctuations. We conclude that prevailing evaluation protocols for augmented LLM systems inadvertently reflect data leakage rather than genuine medical reasoning. To address these systematic artifacts, we propose a rigorous evaluation framework - coupling strict data-isolation protocols with standardized benchmarking safeguards - to ensure future diagnostic AI for rare diseases is evaluated on actual clinical robustness.

infographic.key_insight: Data leakage and evaluation artifacts can substantially inflate apparent rare disease diagnostic performance in augmented LLM systems.
infographic.clinical_relevance: High benchmark accuracy alone does not establish reliable diagnostic performance in real-world clinical settings.
method: Audited evaluation artifacts using over 60,000 cases from public and independent clinical cohorts.
Reconstructed an agentic framework and tested strict cross-dataset isolation alongside supervised classifier evaluations.
Examined retrospective treatment cues and temporal misalignment in foundational knowledge bases.
infographic.evidence_signal: Strict isolation reduced agentic mean Recall@1 from 54.3% to 40.3% (Hedges’ g = 0.94), while supervised classifier accuracy fell from 42.9% internally to 16.7% across external cohorts (Cohen’s d = 2.01).
infographic.watch_item: Real-world clinical utility remains unproven; leakage-controlled benchmarks are necessary but do not substitute for prospective clinical validation.
infographic.paper_title: Auditing evaluation artifacts and data leakage in large language model systems for rare disease diagnosis

title: Toward Clinical Translation of Deep Learning-Based Intracranial Super-Resolution 4D Flow MRI Using Multi-Cohort Transfer Learning
authors: Oliver Welin Odeback, Susanne Schnell, Patrick Winter, Johan Lundberg, Fredrik Piehl, Tobias Granberg
abstract: We evaluated synthetic pretraining and multi-cohort transfer learning for deep learning-based super-resolution of intracranial 4D Flow MRI across heterogeneous neurologic cohorts. This mixed prospective-retrospective study analyzed 18 participants (12 healthy participants, 3 with moyamoya disease, and 3 with multiple sclerosis) with paired 1.2-mm and 0.6-mm 4D Flow MRI scans. A convolutional neural network pretrained on synthetic cerebrovascular data was fine-tuned using cohort-specific or pooled multi-cohort in vivo data. High-resolution-derived inputs enabled voxel-wise evaluation; native standard-resolution scans were used for angiographic and hemodynamic analyses. Synthetic pretraining reduced mean artery-wise velocity-normalized root mean square error (vNRMSE) versus interpolation (0.147 vs 0.166). Pooled transfer learning yielded the lowest mean vNRMSE (0.119 vs 0.127 for cohort-specific models and 0.147 for synthetic pretraining), with narrower 95% limits-of-agreement widths than synthetic pretraining across all test cases (0.109-0.222 vs 0.154-0.278 m/s). Super-resolved phase-contrast angiography achieved higher precision-recall area under the curve than native standard-resolution imaging in all cohorts (0.848-0.896 vs 0.486-0.805). These results indicate that pooled transfer learning improves cross-cohort reconstruction agreement and that super-resolution can improve vessel depiction, supporting further multi-center validation for cerebrovascular imaging.

infographic.key_insight: Pooled multi-cohort transfer learning improved intracranial 4D Flow MRI super-resolution accuracy over cohort-specific training and synthetic pretraining alone.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Improved vessel depiction and velocity reconstruction agreement could support cerebrovascular imaging research, but clinical utility remains unproven.
method: Pretrained a convolutional neural network on synthetic cerebrovascular data.
Fine-tuned with cohort-specific or pooled in vivo MRI data.
Evaluated voxel-wise reconstruction using high-resolution-derived inputs and angiographic performance using native standard-resolution scans.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 18 participants with paired 1.2-mm and 0.6-mm scans, pooled training achieved mean velocity-normalized RMSE of 0.119 versus 0.127 for cohort-specific models and 0.147 for synthetic pretraining.
infographic.watch_item: The small sample—including only three participants each with moyamoya disease and multiple sclerosis—requires larger, multi-center validation.
infographic.paper_title: Toward Clinical Translation of Deep Learning-Based Intracranial Super-Resolution 4D Flow MRI Using Multi-Cohort Transfer Learning

title: Conviction Without Evidence: Verdict Stability Is Independent of Visual Grounding in Medical Vision--Language Models
authors: Federico Felizzi, Francesco Andrea Causio, Bianca Destro Castaniti, Olivia Riccomi, Michele Ferramola, Vittorio De Vita
abstract: Vision--language models applied to medical question answering can reach correct diagnoses without using the diagnostic image, inferring instead from the clinical vignette. We ask whether this is visible in how \emph{firmly} a model holds its answer: does a model defend a diagnosis derived from a blank placeholder as tenaciously as one derived from a real medical image? Crossing an image-substitution protocol with two levels of adversarial pressure on 60 Italian State Examination items, we find no evidence that ungrounded verdicts are more fragile. In a paired item-level analysis, fabricated consensus (L4) overturns 94.4\% of verdicts with the real image and 98.1\% without ($Δ= +0.037$; one-sided 95\% upper bound $+0.105$); contentless doubt (L1) overturns 62.5\% and 51.8\% ($Δ= -0.107$, 95\% CI $[-0.209, -0.001]$), the point estimate running opposite to the direction a grounding detector requires. The two levels nonetheless produce opposite \emph{dynamics}: under L4 the model flips once, always to the exact option argued for (110/110 first-turn flips), and then freezes, averaging 1.9 verdict changes over ten turns; under L1 it never settles, averaging 7.4 changes. Instability under contentless doubt tracks intrinsic item ambiguity rather than evidence availability, and so does not serve as a grounding signal. Flips are almost entirely corrupting (99/100 across both levels). The model is not unaware of the missing evidence---it flags the blank image at baseline on 35 of 60 items and abstains on 4--6---yet those abstentions do not survive contact with pressure. None of the epistemic signals a user could plausibly consult distinguishes a grounded diagnosis from a confabulated one.

infographic.key_insight: Verdict stability did not reliably distinguish diagnoses based on real medical images from those produced with blank placeholders.
infographic.clinical_relevance: A medical vision–language model’s persistence or apparent certainty should not be treated as evidence that it used the diagnostic image.
method: Evaluated 60 Italian State Examination items with real images versus blank placeholders.
Applied contentless doubt (L1) or fabricated consensus (L4) as adversarial pressure.
Compared paired verdict reversals and answer changes over ten turns.
infographic.evidence_signal: Fabricated consensus overturned 94.4% of real-image verdicts versus 98.1% with blank images; contentless doubt overturned 62.5% versus 51.8%, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Findings from this model evaluation on 60 examination items require validation across other models and clinical datasets before broader generalization.
infographic.paper_title: Conviction Without Evidence: Verdict Stability Is Independent of Visual Grounding in Medical Vision--Language Models

title: Multimodal Generative AI Assists Comprehensive Echocardiographic Interpretation
authors: Yi Qin, Marawan Elbatel, Shanshan Song, Taoran Huang, Jiarong Guo, Ningshu Li
abstract: Echocardiography is the cornerstone of cardiovascular diagnostics, yet its global utility is constrained by a critical shortage of experienced interpreters. Current artificial intelligence (AI) solutions remain limited, typically operating as opaque "black boxes" or focusing on narrow tasks that fail to capture the holistic, guideline-driven reasoning of a clinician. Here we introduce EchoChat, a generative multimodal vision-language model that performs comprehensive echocardiographic analysis to support clinician interpretation. By emulating the cognitive workflow of a cardiologist, EchoChat integrates vast medical knowledge with a chain-of-thought reasoning mechanism to explicitly ground its conclusions in visual evidence. Trained on echocardiography-instruction pairs from 46,358 examinations, our model establishes a new state-of-the-art across diverse cohorts from six international medical centers. It supports the broadest diagnostic scope of 33 cardiac conditions and findings, including 15 newly added conditions for which it achieves an average F1 of 73.7% across available external evaluations. It surpasses existing best-performing foundation models in cardiac condition recognition (improving average recall by 13.54% on shared tasks) and quantification (average R2 score increase of 0.275 on shared tasks). Furthermore, in a source-blinded echocardiographer reader study, echocardiography reports co-generated with EchoChat were rated higher in diagnostic accuracy and completeness by two senior echocardiographers, and improved diagnostic performance from 72.78% to 82.75% in terms of F1 score over routine-reader only reports. These results demonstrate that integrating clinical reasoning into multimodal AI can democratize specialist expertise and transform the standard of cardiovascular care.

infographic.key_insight: EchoChat is a multimodal generative AI model that supports comprehensive echocardiographic interpretation across 33 cardiac conditions and findings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: In a source-blinded reader study, EchoChat-assisted reports improved diagnostic F1 from 72.78% to 82.75% compared with routine-reader-only reports.
method: Trained on echocardiography–instruction pairs from 46,358 examinations.
Combines echocardiographic visual evidence with medical knowledge and explicit reasoning.
Evaluated condition recognition, quantification, and clinician-assisted report generation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covered cohorts from six international medical centers; 15 newly added conditions achieved an average F1 of 73.7% across available external evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: Prospective workflow validation is needed before assuming these performance gains translate into safer care or better patient outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: Multimodal Generative AI Assists Comprehensive Echocardiographic Interpretation
